key_terms.meaning: Height of a point above the datum, in m
Fixed point of known RL: GTS, permanent, arbitrary, temporary
RL of the line of collimation: HI = RL + BS; RL = HI − reading
Station read as FS, then as BS after the level moves
e = [(b₂ − a₂) − (b₁ − a₁)] ÷ (D<sub>B</sub> − D<sub>A</sub>); midpoint readings give the true difference
α = s ÷ (nD) rad = 206 265 s ÷ (nD) seconds per division
Observed − known RL of the closing BM; permitted C√K mm (K in km)
Cut = ground RL − formation RL (if positive); fill = formation − ground
ΣBS − ΣFS = last RL − first RL; full: Σ(HI × n) − ΣIS − ΣFS = ΣRL except first
ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last RL − first RL
Reading booked negative; RL = HI + reading size
C = 0.0673 d² m (d in km), subtracted; curvature 0.0785 d², refraction 0.0112 d²
h = ½[(r<sub>B</sub> − r<sub>A</sub>) + (r′<sub>B</sub> − r′<sub>A</sub>)]; e = ½[(r<sub>B</sub> − r<sub>A</sub>) − (r′<sub>B</sub> − r′<sub>A</sub>)]
HE = CI ÷ tan θ = CI × n for a gradient of 1 in n
V = (h/3)[A₁ + A<sub>n</sub> + 4Σ even + 2Σ odd], n odd

takeaways: A level measures only differences of height; the datum enters through a benchmark of known RL.
Within one set-up, RL = HI − reading, and a larger reading means lower ground; an inverted reading is negative.
Temporary adjustments are made at every set-up; the two-peg test checks that the line of collimation is horizontal when the bubble is central.
Equal backsight and foresight lengths cancel collimation error and curvature and refraction.
The arithmetic checks test only arithmetic; closing the run on a known benchmark is the only test of the field work.
Use the full HI check or the rise and fall method when intermediate sights matter.
On long sights subtract 0.0673 d²; across a river use reciprocal levelling.
Close contours mean steep ground; a valley's V points uphill; contours are interpolated from spot levels assuming a uniform slope.
Contour areas give volumes by the trapezoidal or prismoidal rule; capacity is the running sum from the deepest point, and live storage excludes the dead storage below the outlet.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for a full booking and reduction problem (with a change point or an inverted staff), a profile or check levelling problem, the adjustments of a level and the characteristics and uses of contours. Write the formula, substitute, and finish every table with its arithmetic check.

bank.q: Define datum, benchmark, reduced level, backsight, foresight, intermediate sight, change point and height of instrument. Explain, with a sketch, how a reduced level is carried from a GTS benchmark to a distant point.
outline: Datum and MSL; level line versus horizontal line
Four types of benchmark
BS, IS, FS, CP and HI defined
Sketch of set-ups and the height chain
HI = RL + BS; RL = HI − reading; ΣBS − ΣFS check
answer: Datum: the level surface from which heights are measured; in India mean sea level (MSL), to which the Survey of India's benchmarks are referred. A level line lies on a level surface and is curved; a horizontal line is straight and touches the level line at one point. A levelled instrument's line of sight is a horizontal line.
Reduced level (RL): the height of a point above the datum, in metres to three decimals, positive above and negative below the datum.

Benchmark: a fixed point of known RL. GTS benchmarks are fixed by the national survey with published RLs; permanent benchmarks are fixed by departments on culverts, piers and milestones; arbitrary benchmarks are given an assumed RL on small jobs; temporary benchmarks are set for one job, to close and restart work.

Backsight (BS): the first reading after setting up, on a point of known RL. Foresight (FS): the last reading before the level is moved. Intermediate sight (IS): any reading between them. Change point (CP): a firm point that takes an FS from one set-up and a BS from the next. Height of instrument (HI): the RL of the line of collimation for a set-up.

answer.text: Sketch (side view): the GTS BM, the level at set-up 1 with its horizontal line of sight, the staff on CP1, set-up 2, and the staff on the distant point P. Each set-up has its own HI.

svg.aria: Two level set-ups carrying a height from a benchmark through a change point to a point P

answer: Procedure: set up between the BM and CP1 with roughly equal sights; HI₁ = RL(BM) + BS₁; RL(CP1) = HI₁ − FS₁. Move the level; HI₂ = RL(CP1) + BS₂; RL(P) = HI₂ − FS₂. Repeat for as many set-ups as needed.
Worked numbers: BM 120.450 m, BS 1.865 → HI 122.315 m; FS 1.250 on a TBM → RL 121.065 m. The TBM is then the start of the next day's work.

Check: ΣBS − ΣFS = RL(last) − RL(first). Here 1.865 − 1.250 = 0.615 = 121.065 − 120.450. The run should finally close on a second known benchmark so that the field work, not just the arithmetic, is checked.

bank.q: Describe the temporary adjustments of a dumpy level. State the fundamental lines and the permanent adjustments, and explain the principle of the two-peg test.
outline: Setting up, levelling up (two screws, then third), eyepiece, objective, parallax
Vertical axis, bubble axis, line of collimation and required relations
Bubble tube, cross-hair ring and collimation adjustments in order
Two-peg test: midpoint gives true difference; second set-up finds the error
answer: Setting up: plant the tripod legs firmly and bring the head roughly level by moving the legs; fix the instrument.

Levelling up: turn the telescope parallel to two foot screws and turn them together, thumbs both inward or both outward, until the bubble is central (it follows the left thumb). Turn the telescope through 90° over the third screw and centre the bubble with it alone. Repeat until the bubble stays central in every direction.

Focusing the eyepiece on the cross-hairs against a bright background; focusing the objective on the staff; removing parallax by refocusing until the cross-hair does not move on the staff when the eye moves.

Fundamental lines: the vertical axis, the axis of the bubble tube and the line of collimation. Required: bubble axis ⟂ vertical axis; line of collimation ∥ bubble axis; horizontal cross-hair ⟂ vertical axis.
Bubble tube adjustment: level up, turn through 180°; if the bubble runs, correct half with the capstan screws of the tube and half with the foot screws; repeat.
Cross-hair ring adjustment: a point at one end of the horizontal hair must stay on the hair as the telescope turns; if not, rotate the diaphragm ring.
Collimation adjustment by the two-peg test. Pegs A and B about 100 m apart. With the level midway, both sights are equal, so their errors are equal and b₁ − a₁ is the true difference.

Set up at D close to one peg (on the line produced) and read both again. With e the error per metre: (b₂ − D<sub>B</sub>e) − (a₂ − D<sub>A</sub>e) = b₁ − a₁, so e = [(b₂ − a₂) − (b₁ − a₁)] ÷ (D<sub>B</sub> − D<sub>A</sub>).

Example: b₁ − a₁ = 2.115 − 1.625 = 0.490 m; from D (10 m beyond A, 110 m from B) b₂ − a₂ = 1.943 − 1.435 = 0.508 m; e = 0.018 ÷ 100 = 0.00018 per m, upward (about 37″). Correct reading on B = 1.943 − 110 × 0.00018 = 1.923 m.

Adjust: on a dumpy level move the diaphragm until B reads 1.923 m with the bubble central; on a tilting level set 1.923 m with the tilting screw and re-centre the bubble with its capstan screws. Check: corrected readings 1.923 − 1.433 = 0.490 m, the true difference.

bank.q: State the characteristics of contours. Describe the direct and indirect methods of contouring and list the uses of a contour map.
outline: Contour, contour interval, horizontal equivalent
Six or more characteristics with valley and ridge
Direct method with the staff reading HI − H
Indirect: grid, cross-sections, radial, tacheometric; interpolation
Uses: sections, intervisibility, grade contour, catchment, reservoir, earthwork
answer: A contour joins points of equal RL. The contour interval (CI) is the constant RL step between contours; the horizontal equivalent (HE) is the plan distance between two contours, HE = CI ÷ tan θ = CI × n for a gradient of 1 in n.

Characteristics: every point on a contour has the same RL; every contour closes, on or off the map; close spacing means steep ground, wide spacing gentle ground, equal spacing a uniform slope; contours of different RL never cross except at an overhang and merge only at a vertical cliff; closed loops with higher values inside are hills, with lower values inside depressions; across a valley the V points uphill, across a ridge downhill; the steepest slope (water flow) is at right angles to the contours.

Direct method: set up the level, take a BS on a BM and find HI. For a contour of RL H the staff must read HI − H. Example: HI 101.235 m → 1.235 m for the 100 m contour, 0.735 m for 100.5 m. The staffman moves until the reading matches; the point is pegged and fixed in plan. Accurate but slow; for small, open sites.

Indirect method: spot levels are taken and contours are interpolated. Layouts: a grid of squares (block levelling, 5 to 20 m) on small gentle sites; cross-sections along a route; radial lines from a central station on hills; tacheometric points on rough ground.

Interpolation by calculation: x = L (H − H<sub>A</sub>) ÷ (H<sub>B</sub> − H<sub>A</sub>). Example: A 102.6 m and B 105.1 m, 30 m apart; the 104 m contour is 30 × 1.4 ÷ 2.5 = 16.8 m from A. Estimation and the graphical method are quicker and rougher.
Choice of CI: purpose, map scale, steepness of the ground, time and cost; 0.25 to 1 m on site plans, 10 to 20 m on 1:50 000 sheets.

Uses: drawing a longitudinal or cross-section along any line; testing intervisibility; locating a route at a fixed gradient by stepping the HE with dividers (1 in 25 with a 2 m CI → 50 m, 20 mm at 1:2500); marking the catchment; finding the submerged area and capacity of a reservoir; estimating cut and fill; choosing sites for buildings, dams and bridges.

bank.q: Explain simple, differential, fly, check and profile levelling. What are the sources of error in levelling and the precautions against them?
outline: Simple: one set-up; differential: change points
Fly: quick BS/FS run; check: closes on a known BM; permissible error C√K
Profile: L-section and cross-sections, IS at pegs
Instrumental, natural and personal errors
Precautions
answer: Simple levelling: both points seen from one set-up; difference = BS − FS.

Differential (compound) levelling: used when points are far apart, at very different heights or hidden; the run is split by change points read first as FS then as BS. Check ΣBS − ΣFS = last RL − first RL.
Fly levelling: a quick differential run with long, balanced sights and only BS and FS, to carry a benchmark's height to the site.

Check levelling: a run made to test earlier work; it closes on the starting BM or on another BM. Closing error e = observed − known RL; permissible e = C√K mm (K in km), C set by the class of work. Example: run of 1.6 km closing +12 mm with 12√K allowed: limit 15.2 mm, accepted; corrections −3 mm per set-up.

Profile levelling: RLs along a centre line at 20 m or 30 m pegs (intermediate sights) plotted as a longitudinal section with an exaggerated vertical scale; cross-sections at right angles at each peg. The formation line drawn on it gives depths of cut and fill.
Instrumental errors: line of collimation not horizontal with the bubble central; sluggish bubble; loose tripod head; staff of wrong length or worn foot.
Natural errors: curvature and refraction on long sights (0.0673 d²); wind shaking the staff; heat shimmer; settlement of the tripod or of a change point.
Personal errors: bubble not central while reading; parallax; staff not vertical (reads too large); misreading metres or decimetres; booking in the wrong column or row.

Precautions: sights under about 100 m and balanced; bubble checked at each reading; staff rocked and the least reading taken; change points on firm, sharp objects; readings booked at once and the arithmetic check done on site; every run closed on a known benchmark.

Sketch for the answer: a longitudinal section with the ground line, the formation line, and cut shaded where the ground is above it and fill where it is below; with the HI method each peg's RL is HI − IS.
Typical class of work: the constant C in C√K is a few millimetres for precise levelling and larger for ordinary engineering levelling; the specification of the job fixes it.

bank.q: The following consecutive readings were taken with a level and a 4 m staff: 0.865 (BM, RL 200.000 m), 1.705, 2.440, 3.125, 1.385, 0.950, 1.630, 2.890, 2.215, 1.475, 0.780 (TBM). The instrument was shifted after the fourth and the eighth readings. Book the readings, reduce by the height of collimation method and apply all checks.
outline: Identify BS, IS, FS and the two change points
HI per set-up and RLs
Check ΣBS − ΣFS = last − first
Full HI check including intermediate sights
answer: Classify: reading 1 is a BS on the BM. The instrument moved after readings 4 and 8, so 3.125 (4th) and 2.890 (8th) are foresights on change points, and the readings after them, 1.385 and 2.215, are backsights on the same points. Others are intermediate sights; the last, 0.780, is an FS.

answer.text: Full check, which also tests the intermediate sights: each HI times the number of readings reduced from it (3, 3 and 2):

answer: Both checks balance. The TBM is 2.330 m below the BM, at RL 197.670 m.
Classification rule used: the first reading after every move is a BS, the last reading before every move is an FS, and the very last reading of the run is always an FS; everything else is an IS.
Why the full check matters here: Check 1 uses only the three BS and three FS values, so a slip in the five intermediate RLs (A, B, C, D, E) would pass it; the full check uses every reduced level.
Rise and fall cross-check (optional): 0.865 → 1.705 fall 0.840 gives A = 199.160 m, the same as the HI method; ΣRise − ΣFall = 1.870 − 4.200 = −2.330 m.

bank.q: In a building, a level was set up to transfer a level from a BM (RL 45.250 m) outside. Readings: 1.450 on the BM; 1.120 on the floor; −2.265 with the staff inverted on the underside of a roof beam; 1.890 on CP1 (then the level was moved); 0.985 on CP1; 2.640 on P; 3.365 on Q; 3.810 on CP2 (moved); 1.240 on CP2; 0.655 on a TBM. Reduce by the rise and fall method, apply the check, and find the headroom under the beam.
outline: Book with CP lines and the inverted reading
Rises and falls with signs, including −2.265
RLs
Check
Headroom = beam RL − floor RL
answer: Compare each reading with the previous one of the same set-up: previous − present, positive = rise, negative = fall.
Headroom under the beam = 48.965 − 45.580 = 3.385 m (the rise from the floor to the beam).

Why the inverted reading is negative: the beam is above the line of sight, so the staff's zero is up against the beam and the cross-hair reads 2.265 m below it; with HI 46.700 m the beam is at 46.700 + 2.265 = 48.965 m. In rise and fall the minus sign is kept in the subtraction: 1.120 − (−2.265) = 3.385 m rise.
Common slips to avoid: booking CP1 on two lines, comparing 0.985 with −2.265 instead of with 2.640, and dropping the minus sign, which would put the beam 4.530 m too low.

bank.q: In a two-peg test, pegs A and B are 120 m apart. With the level midway, the readings are 1.784 m on A and 1.326 m on B. The level is then set up at D on the line AB produced, 12 m beyond B, and the readings are 1.540 m on A and 1.094 m on B. Find the true difference of level, the collimation error and its direction, and the readings on A and B for a correct line of sight from D.
outline: True difference from the midpoint
Apparent difference from D
e from the difference over D<sub>A</sub> − D<sub>B</sub>
Direction and angle
Corrected readings and check
answer: From the midpoint the errors cancel: b₁ − a₁ = 1.326 − 1.784 = −0.458 m, so B is 0.458 m higher than A.
From D: D<sub>A</sub> = 132 m, D<sub>B</sub> = 12 m. Apparent b₂ − a₂ = 1.094 − 1.540 = −0.446 m.
Negative e means the readings are too small: the line of sight is inclined downward. Angle = 0.0001 × 206 265 ≈ 21″.
Check: 1.095 − 1.553 = −0.458 m, the true difference.

Adjustment: with the level at D and the bubble central, raise the line of sight (diaphragm on a dumpy level, or tilting screw then bubble capstan screws on a tilting level) until A reads 1.553 m; repeat the test to confirm.
Effect if not adjusted: with a 30 m backsight and a 60 m foresight, the error in the difference would be 30 × 0.0001 = 3 mm per set-up, which is why sights are balanced.
Why the midpoint gives the true difference: both sights are 60 m, so both readings are too small by 60 × 0.0001 = 0.006 m and the difference is unaffected.

Why D is placed close to one peg: the near reading then carries very little error (here 12 × 0.0001 = 0.0012 m), so the far reading shows almost all of it; the formula still corrects both readings exactly.
Sketch: the two side views, level midway and level at D, with the true horizontal dashed and the inclined line of sight drawn below it towards A.
Order of permanent adjustments: the bubble tube and cross-hair ring adjustments are done before this test, because the test assumes the bubble axis is perpendicular to the vertical axis.

Summary of results: true difference 0.458 m (B higher); collimation error 0.0001 per metre, line of sight inclined downward by about 21″; from D the staff should read 1.553 m on A and 1.095 m on B. A 0.012 m discrepancy over the 120 m difference in sight lengths is what the test detects; the arithmetic is the same whichever peg the level is placed near, provided D<sub>A</sub> and D<sub>B</sub> are measured from the level.

bank.q: Reciprocal levelling across a valley 1.2 km wide gave: level near A, staff on A 0.985 m and on B 2.720 m; level near B, staff on B 1.900 m and on A 0.375 m. The RL of A is 312.450 m. Find the RL of B, the combined curvature and refraction correction, and the collimation error. Also find the distance to the visible horizon from a station 9 m above the level surface.
outline: Apparent differences from each side
Mean = true difference; half-difference = far-sight error
Collimation = e − C, angle
Horizon d = 3.855√h
answer: From near A: r<sub>B</sub> − r<sub>A</sub> = 2.720 − 0.985 = 1.735 m. From near B: r′<sub>B</sub> − r′<sub>A</sub> = 1.900 − 0.375 = 1.525 m.
True difference h = ½(1.735 + 1.525) = 1.630 m; positive, so B is lower than A.
Error in one far reading e = ½(1.735 − 1.525) = 0.105 m.
Combined correction for d = 1.2 km: C = 0.0673 × 1.44 = 0.097 m (curvature 0.0785 × 1.44 = 0.113 m less refraction 0.016 m).
Collimation error over 1.2 km = 0.105 − 0.097 = 0.008 m, readings too high, so the line of sight points upward by 0.008 ÷ 1200 × 206 265 ≈ 1.4″.

Why the method works: near readings carry almost no error; the far reading carries +e from both sides, so the mean of the two apparent differences cancels e (curvature, refraction and collimation), provided refraction is the same for both far sights.
Visible horizon from h = 9 m: d = √(9 ÷ 0.0673) = 3.855 × √9 = 11.6 km.
Check: C at 11.6 km = 0.0673 × 11.6² = 9.06 m ≈ 9 m, the height of the station.
Sketch: the valley with A and B; the level a few metres from A reading A (near) and B (far), then a few metres from B reading B (near) and A (far); the far sights both run 1.2 km.
Sign check: B lower means the readings on B exceed those on A from both set-ups, as found (1.735 and 1.525 are both positive).
Practical note: refraction varies with temperature near the ground, so the two sets should be taken at about the same time of day (ideally simultaneously with two levels) and several sets averaged.
Comparison: without reciprocal levelling, the single set-up near A would give B lower by 1.735 m, an error of 0.105 m; applying C alone would leave 0.008 m of collimation error.

Summary: RL of B 310.820 m; far-sight error 0.105 m, made up of 0.097 m curvature and refraction and 0.008 m collimation (about 1.4″ upward). The result does not depend on the instrument height at either bank, because each set-up's two readings are taken with the same line of sight.

bank.q: Profile levelling along a proposed drain at 30 m intervals gave: BS 2.155 on a BM of RL 120.500 m; IS 1.640 (ch 0), 1.215 (ch 30), 0.790 (ch 60); FS 0.325 (ch 90, change point); BS 2.580 (ch 90); IS 1.960 (ch 120), 1.395 (ch 150); FS 0.810 (ch 180). The formation starts at RL 121.300 m at ch 0 and rises at 1 in 100. Reduce the levels, find the depths of cut and fill, and the chainage of the zero point.
outline: HI per set-up and ground RLs
Arithmetic check
Formation RLs
Cut/fill table
Zero point by interpolation
answer: Interpretation: the ground rises at about 1 in 58 (3.085 m in 180 m), steeper than the drain at 1 in 100, so the drain is in filling at the start and in increasing cutting beyond about 66 m, reaching 1.000 m at ch 180.
Plot ground and formation against chainage with the vertical scale exaggerated to show the cut and fill areas.
Booking used: height of collimation method, because six of the eight readings are intermediate sights on pegs.

answer: Checks on the answer: the cut and fill change sign once, between 60 m and 90 m, as the zero-point calculation assumes; the last depth (1.000 m cut at 180 m) equals 124.100 − 123.100. Cross-sections at each peg would then give the width of cut or bank for the earthwork quantities.

bank.q: The areas inside the contours of a proposed reservoir are: 250 m, 12 000 m²; 253 m, 46 000 m²; 256 m, 98 000 m²; 259 m, 165 000 m²; 262 m, 252 000 m². The deepest point is at RL 248.2 m. Find the capacity at each contour, and compare the trapezoidal and prismoidal volumes between 250 m and 262 m.
outline: Contour interval 3 m
Bottom cone
Slices by the end-area rule and running sums
Trapezoidal and prismoidal totals
Comment on the difference
answer: Contour interval h = 3 m; five contours, so four slices (an odd number of contours, as the prismoidal rule needs).
Below 250 m, to the deepest point 248.2 m: cone V₀ = 12 000 × 1.8 ÷ 3 = 7200 m³.
Difference = 19 000 m³, about 1.5 %. The trapezoidal rule overestimates when the area grows faster than linearly with height, as in a widening valley; the prismoidal value is preferred.
Capacity at 262 m by the prismoidal rule plus the cone = 1 304 000 + 7 200 = 1 311 200 m³ (1.31 million m³).
Use: plot capacity against RL to read the storage at any water level; storage between two levels = difference of the two capacities, e.g. 253 to 259 m = 704 700 − 94 200 = 610 500 m³.
Units: 1 ha = 10 000 m², so the capacity at 262 m is about 131 ha·m.

Why the cone: the lowest contour does not reach the deepest point; the water between 248.2 m and 250 m (7200 m³) belongs in the capacity, so it is added as a cone with base 12 000 m² and height 1.8 m.
Accuracy of the areas: they come from a planimeter or coordinates on the contour plan, and any error in them passes straight into the volumes; contours at a closer interval improve both rules.

bank.q: A 1.2 km road is to be levelled for its longitudinal section. Heights must be brought from a GTS benchmark (RL 54.215 m) 0.6 km away to a site TBM, checked, and then used for the profile. A check run of six set-ups (2.25 km) gave the TBM as 57.880 m after three set-ups and closed on the GTS benchmark at 54.199 m. With a permitted error of 12√K mm, evaluate the run, correct the TBM, and justify the methods and booking you would use for the whole job.
outline: Fly levelling out, check levelling back
Closing error and permitted limit
Distribution of correction
Profile with HI booking; check run with rise and fall
Field precautions and plan
answer: Closing error e = observed − known = 54.199 − 54.215 = −0.016 m (−16 mm).
Permitted error = 12√2.25 = 12 × 1.5 = 18 mm. Since 16 mm < 18 mm, the run is accepted.
Correction = +16 mm shared over six set-ups = +2.67 mm per set-up. The TBM was reached after three set-ups: correction = +3 × 2.67 = +8 mm. Corrected RL of TBM = 57.880 + 0.008 = 57.888 m.

Method to the site: fly levelling (backsights and foresights only, balanced sights of 50 to 80 m) from the GTS BM to the TBM, then check levelling back to the BM or on to a second benchmark, so that field mistakes show as a misclosure; the arithmetic check alone cannot show them.
Booking for the check run: rise and fall, because its check ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last − first covers every reading.

Profile: pegs every 20 m or 30 m on the 1.2 km centre line and at changes of slope; from each set-up a BS on the TBM or a CP, intermediate sights on every peg in view, and an FS on a CP. Booking by the height of collimation method, because there are many intermediate sights; apply Check 1 and the full HI check. Close the profile run on the TBM or a second TBM.
Cross-sections at each peg at set offsets to give the road width for earthwork.

Precautions: test the level by the two-peg test before starting; keep sights under about 100 m and balanced; change points on firm plates; avoid midday shimmer; staff vertical and read without parallax.
Result: TBM 57.888 m (accepted, error −16 mm within 18 mm). Had the error exceeded 18 mm, the run would be repeated, not adjusted.
Check of the correction sum: the six set-up corrections (+2.67 mm each) add to +16 mm, cancelling the closing error exactly.
If the set-ups were of very unequal length, the correction would be shared in proportion to distance instead: correction at a point = −e × (distance to it ÷ total distance).
Record keeping: book the TBM's corrected RL (57.888 m) with its description and sketch, so later work starts from the adjusted value.

bank.q: A site was block-levelled on 10 m squares. Row P: P1 48.6, P2 49.4, P3 50.3; row Q: Q1 47.9, Q2 48.8, Q3 49.7; row R: R1 47.2, R2 48.1, R3 48.9 m. Interpolate the 48, 49 and 50 m contours, describe the ground, and compare this method with direct contouring for the same site (HI 50.215 m).
outline: Which grid lines each contour crosses
Distances by x = L(H − H₁)/(H₂ − H₁)
Joining the points; shape of ground
Direct method staff readings
Comparison of accuracy, speed and suitability
answer: A contour crosses a grid line only when the line's two RLs lie on opposite sides of its value. Distance from the first point: x = 10 (H − H₁) ÷ (H₂ − H₁).
Join in each square: 48 m runs P1–Q1 → Q1–Q2 → R1–R2; 49 m runs P1–P2 → P2–Q2 → Q2–Q3 → Q3–R3; 50 m cuts the corner P2–P3 → P3–Q3.

Ground: RL rises from R1 (47.2) to P3 (50.3), 3.1 m over the 28.3 m diagonal, about 1 in 9; contours run from north-west to south-east, roughly evenly spaced, so the slope is fairly uniform and faces south-west.
Direct contouring from HI 50.215 m: staff readings 2.215 m (48 m), 1.215 m (49 m) and 0.215 m (50 m); the staffman finds each point on the ground and it is pegged and fixed in plan.

Comparison: the direct method locates the contours on the actual ground, so it is more accurate where the slope is irregular, but slow; the grid (indirect) method is faster, needs simple field work and also gives spot levels for earthwork, but assumes a uniform slope between grid points.
Evaluation: for this small, gentle, open site a 10 m grid is the better choice; direct contouring suits a reservoir rim or a building plot where a particular contour must be marked on the ground.
Interpolation assumption: the ground slopes uniformly between neighbouring grid points; a hump or hollow between points is missed, so the grid spacing is chosen to suit the roughness of the ground.
Sketch: the 3 × 3 grid with its spot levels and the three contour lines through the crossing points.
